title: Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics for Data Discovery
text:
This report investigates a real-world motor vehicle insurance portfolio from Spain to identify the main drivers of portfolio profitability and volatility. Following the take-home brief, the analysis uses tidyverse for data processing and ggplot2 plus its extensions for visual analytics.
The core business questions are:

Which policy, customer and vehicle segments are associated with weaker profitability?
Which segments show higher claim volatility through elevated claim frequency or claim severity?
What actions should an insurer prioritise to improve portfolio performance?

pacman::p_load(tidyverse, patchwork, ggdist, ggridges, scales, knitr, readxl)

portfolio <- prepare_motor_data("../../data/motor_insurance_portfolio.csv")

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics for Data Discovery
text:
Data Preparation

Wrangling Workflow
The analytical sandbox was prepared with the following steps:

Import the semicolon-delimited CSV using read_delim().
Validate the 47 variables against the accompanying codebook.
Derive business metrics required by the brief:

loss_ratio = total_incurred / total_premium
claim_frequency = total_claims / total_exposure
claim_severity = total_incurred / total_claims
premium_per_exposure, pure_premium, total_margin
age and value bands for interpretable segmentation

Cap loss_ratio and claim_frequency at the 99th percentile for distribution plots, while keeping uncapped values for aggregated portfolio metrics.
Retain the 49 records with zero premium and zero exposure in the base data, but exclude them automatically from ratio calculations to avoid infinite results.

  dplyr::filter(!is.na(Variables)) |>

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics for Data Discovery
text:
Executive Summary of Findings
Four messages stand out from the analysis:

Comprehensive products drive the weakest profitability. COMP_N has the highest claim frequency and loss ratio, and its loss ratio exceeded 1.0 in 2024.
Portfolio renewals underperform new business. The existing portfolio segment shows consistently higher claim incidence, claim frequency and loss ratio than new business.
Billing cadence and underwriting quality matter. Semiannual and quarterly payment plans perform worse than annual plans, while favourable bonus scores materially reduce claim risk.
The portfolio deteriorated in 2024. Loss ratio rose to roughly 74.7% in 2024 from about 65.6% in 2022, indicating worsening profitability despite only modest movement in claim severity.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics for Data Discovery
text:
Univariate Visual Analytics

Portfolio Mix by Exposure


Code
mix_tbl <- portfolio |>
  dplyr::group_by(policy_type) |>
  dplyr::summarise(exposure = sum(total_exposure, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  dplyr::mutate(exposure_share = exposure / sum(exposure)) |>
  dplyr::arrange(desc(exposure_share))

mix_plot <- ggplot(mix_tbl, aes(x = forcats::fct_reorder(policy_type, exposure_share), y = exposure_share, fill = policy_type)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(exposure_share, accuracy = 0.1)), hjust = -0.1, size = 3.6) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = portfolio_cols) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.08))) +
  labs(
    title = "Exposure is concentrated in CC and COMP_E policies",
    subtitle = "Policy mix should be read in exposure terms rather than raw policy counts",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Exposure share"
  ) +
  portfolio_theme()

mix_plot









The portfolio is structurally concentrated in CC and COMP_E. This matters because portfolio profitability can be heavily influenced by the performance of these dominant product lines.


Distribution of Key Numeric Variables


Code
age_plot <- ggplot(portfolio, aes(x = driver_age)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 3, fill = accent_cols["primary"], colour = "white", alpha = 0.9) +
  labs(title = "Driver ages cluster in mature segments", x = "Driver age", y = "Policies") +
  portfolio_theme()

value_plot <- ggplot(portfolio, aes(x = vehicle_value)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5000, fill = accent_cols["secondary"], colour = "white", alpha = 0.9) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar(prefix = "EUR ", accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(title = "Vehicle values are strongly right-skewed", x = "Vehicle value", y = "Policies") +
  portfolio_theme()

premium_plot <- ggplot(portfolio, aes(x = total_premium)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 25, fill = accent_cols["highlight"], colour = "white", alpha = 0.9) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1200)) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar(prefix = "EUR ", accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(title = "Most premiums sit in the lower-price range", x = "Total premium", y = "Policies") +
  portfolio_theme()

(age_plot | value_plot) / premium_plot









The numerical variables reveal a mature driver base, very skewed vehicle values, and a premium distribution concentrated at lower price points. These shapes justify the use of robust visual summaries and non-parametric statistical tests later in the report.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics for Data Discovery
text:
Bivariate Visual Analytics for Profitability

Policy Type is the Strongest Profitability Driver


Code
policy_perf <- segment_metrics(portfolio, "policy_type") |>
  dplyr::mutate(group = forcats::fct_reorder(group, loss_ratio))

policy_lr_plot <- ggplot(policy_perf, aes(x = group, y = loss_ratio, fill = group)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(loss_ratio, accuracy = 0.1)), vjust = -0.25, size = 3.3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = portfolio_cols) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.08))) +
  labs(
    title = "Comprehensive products record the weakest profitability",
    subtitle = "Exposure-weighted loss ratio by policy type",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Loss ratio"
  ) +
  portfolio_theme()

policy_freq_plot <- ggplot(policy_perf, aes(x = group, y = claim_frequency, fill = group)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::number(claim_frequency, accuracy = 0.01)), vjust = -0.25, size = 3.3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = portfolio_cols) +
  labs(
    title = "Claim frequency follows the same pattern",
    subtitle = "Claims per unit of exposure by policy type",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Claim frequency"
  ) +
  portfolio_theme()

policy_lr_plot | policy_freq_plot









COMP_N is the least profitable segment, with the highest exposure-adjusted claim frequency and the highest loss ratio. At the other end, TP is materially more profitable. This suggests that product design, coverage breadth and pricing structure are central portfolio levers.


Profitability Deteriorated in 2024


Code
year_type_tbl <- portfolio |>
  dplyr::group_by(year, policy_type) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    exposure = sum(total_exposure, na.rm = TRUE),
    loss_ratio = sum(total_incurred, na.rm = TRUE) / sum(total_premium, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(year_type_tbl, aes(x = factor(year), y = policy_type, fill = loss_ratio)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(loss_ratio, accuracy = 0.1)), size = 3.2) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#d9f0f3", high = "#9d0208", labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  labs(
    title = "2024 shows a broad-based profitability deterioration",
    subtitle = "Loss ratio by year and policy type",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    fill = "Loss ratio"
  ) +
  portfolio_theme()









The worsening in 2024 is not isolated to one niche segment. It is strongest in comprehensive covers, especially COMP_N, where the loss ratio crossed the breakeven threshold of 100%.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics for Data Discovery
text:
Bivariate Visual Analytics for Volatility

Volatility is Elevated in Comprehensive Covers


Code
dist_sample <- sample_for_distribution(portfolio, n = 50000)

ggplot(
  dist_sample |>
    dplyr::filter(policy_type %in% c("TP", "TPG", "CC", "COMP_E", "COMP_N")),
  aes(x = policy_type, y = claim_severity, fill = policy_type)
) +
  ggdist::stat_halfeye(
    adjust = 0.5,
    width = 0.6,
    .width = c(0.5, 0.8, 0.95),
    justification = -0.25,
    point_colour = NA
  ) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.12, outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.45) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = portfolio_cols) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_dollar(prefix = "EUR ", accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Claim severity is both high and dispersed in comprehensive segments",
    subtitle = "Half-eye + boxplot of claim severity on a log scale",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Claim severity"
  ) +
  portfolio_theme()









Volatility is not just about average loss ratio. The half-eye distributions show that comprehensive products also carry wider severity spreads, which creates higher earnings uncertainty even when average profitability looks manageable.


Billing Frequency and Underwriting Quality Segment the Risk


Code
billing_tbl <- segment_metrics(portfolio, "payment_frequency") |>
  dplyr::mutate(group = forcats::fct_relevel(group, "A", "S", "Q"))

bonus_tbl <- segment_metrics(portfolio, "bonus_score") |>
  dplyr::mutate(group = forcats::fct_relevel(group, "G", "N", "B"))

billing_plot <- ggplot(billing_tbl, aes(x = group, y = loss_ratio, fill = group)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(loss_ratio, accuracy = 0.1)), vjust = -0.2, size = 3.3) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.08))) +
  labs(title = "Annual billing performs best", x = "Payment frequency", y = "Loss ratio") +
  portfolio_theme()

bonus_plot <- ggplot(bonus_tbl, aes(x = group, y = claim_frequency, fill = group)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::number(claim_frequency, accuracy = 0.01)), vjust = -0.2, size = 3.3) +
  labs(title = "Favourable bonus scores reduce claim frequency", x = "Bonus score", y = "Claim frequency") +
  portfolio_theme()

billing_plot | bonus_plot









Payment cadence and bonus score are practical underwriting signals. Annual billing is materially more profitable than semiannual or quarterly billing, while G bonus scores clearly outperform N and B.


Vehicle Value and Driver Age Refine the Story


Code
age_value_tbl <- portfolio |>
  dplyr::group_by(driver_age_band, vehicle_value_band) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    exposure = sum(total_exposure, na.rm = TRUE),
    loss_ratio = sum(total_incurred, na.rm = TRUE) / sum(total_premium, na.rm = TRUE),
    claim_frequency = sum(total_claims, na.rm = TRUE) / sum(total_exposure, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(driver_age_band), !is.na(vehicle_value_band))

ggplot(age_value_tbl, aes(x = driver_age_band, y = vehicle_value_band)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = exposure, colour = loss_ratio)) +
  scale_size_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  scale_colour_gradient(low = "#94d2bd", high = "#9d0208", labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  labs(
    title = "High-value vehicles push profitability downward across age bands",
    subtitle = "Bubble size encodes exposure; colour encodes loss ratio",
    x = "Driver age band",
    y = "Vehicle value band",
    size = "Exposure",
    colour = "Loss ratio"
  ) +
  portfolio_theme()









Higher vehicle values are associated with weaker profitability across most age bands. Younger drivers have the highest claim frequency, but the broader profitability problem is not limited to youth; it also appears in large mature segments exposed to high-value vehicles.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics for Data Discovery
text:
Recommendations
Based on the visual analytics evidence, the insurer should prioritise five actions:

Reprice or redesign comprehensive covers, especially COMP_N, because they combine weak profitability with high volatility.
Review portfolio renewals more closely than new business, since the existing portfolio carries worse frequency and profitability outcomes.
Promote annual billing and review surcharges on instalment plans, because quarterly and semiannual billing underperform.
Use bonus score more aggressively in underwriting and retention, as favourable claims history is one of the clearest risk separators.
Drill into the 2024 deterioration, especially within comprehensive products and high-value vehicles, to distinguish pricing drift from claims inflation.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics for Data Discovery
text:
Conclusion
This take-home exercise shows how visual analytics helps move beyond dashboard reporting into portfolio discovery. The portfolio is dominated by a few product lines, and those product lines do not perform equally. Comprehensive covers, portfolio renewals, non-annual billing, weak bonus scores and higher-value vehicles all contribute to lower profitability or higher volatility. Just as importantly, the deterioration observed in 2024 suggests that the insurer should treat the problem as dynamic rather than static.

title: Hands-on Exercise 3: Interactive and Animated Data Visualisation
text:
3.3 Interactive Visualisation - ggiraph methods

3.3.1 Tooltip effect

p <- ggplot(data = exam_data,
            aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(
    aes(tooltip = ID),
    stackgroups = TRUE,
    binwidth = 1,
    method = "histodot") +
  scale_y_continuous(NULL,
                     breaks = NULL)

girafe(
  ggobj = p,
  width_svg = 6,
  height_svg = 6 * 0.618
)







3.3.2 Displaying multiple information on tooltip

exam_data$tooltip <- c(paste0(
  "Name = ", exam_data$ID,
  "\n Class = ", exam_data$CLASS))


p <- ggplot(data = exam_data,
            aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(
    aes(tooltip = exam_data$tooltip),
    stackgroups = TRUE,
    binwidth = 1,
    method = "histodot") +
  scale_y_continuous(NULL,
                     breaks = NULL)

girafe(
  ggobj = p,
  width_svg = 8,
  height_svg = 8 * 0.618
)







3.3.3 Customising tooltip style

tooltip_css <- "background-color:white;
font-style:bold; color:black;"


p <- ggplot(data = exam_data,
            aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(
    aes(tooltip = ID),
    stackgroups = TRUE,
    binwidth = 1,
    method = "histodot") +
  scale_y_continuous(NULL,
                     breaks = NULL)

girafe(
  ggobj = p,
  width_svg = 6,
  height_svg = 6 * 0.618,
  options = list(
    opts_tooltip(css = tooltip_css))
)







3.3.4 Displaying statistics on tooltip

tooltip <- function(y, ymax, accuracy = .01) {
  mean <- scales::number(y, accuracy = accuracy)
  sem  <- scales::number(ymax - y, accuracy = accuracy)
  paste("Mean maths scores:", mean, "+/-", sem)
}


gg_point <- ggplot(data = exam_data,
                   aes(x = RACE)) +
  stat_summary(aes(y = MATHS,
                   tooltip = after_stat(
                     tooltip(y, ymax))),
               fun.data = "mean_se",
               geom = GeomInteractiveCol,
               fill = "light blue") +
  stat_summary(aes(y = MATHS),
               fun.data = mean_se,
               geom = "errorbar",
               width = 0.2,
               size = 0.2)

girafe(ggobj = gg_point,
       width_svg = 8,
       height_svg = 8 * 0.618)

p <- ggplot(data = exam_data,
            aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(
    aes(data_id = CLASS),
    stackgroups = TRUE,
    binwidth = 1,
    method = "histodot") +

girafe(

  width_svg = 6,

p <- ggplot(data = exam_data,
            aes(x = MATHS)) +

  numerator = Death,
  denominator = Positive,
  group = `Sub-district`,
  data_type = "PR",
  xrange = c(0, 6500),
  yrange = c(0, 0.05),
  label = NA,
  title = "Cumulative COVID-19 Fatality Rate by Cumulative Total Number of COVID-19 Positive Cases",
  x_label = "Cumulative COVID-19 Positive Cases",
  y_label = "Cumulative Fatality Rate"
)








A funnel plot object with 267 points of which 7 are outliers. 
Plot is adjusted for overdispersion. 









df <- covid19 %>%
  mutate(rate = Death / Positive) %>%
  mutate(rate.se = sqrt((rate * (1 - rate)) / Positive)) %>%
  filter(rate > 0)

fit.mean <- weighted.mean(df$rate, 1 / df$rate.se^2)





number.seq <- seq(1, max(df$Positive), 1)
number.ll95 <- fit.mean - 1.96 * sqrt((fit.mean * (1 - fit.mean)) / number.seq)
number.ul95 <- fit.mean + 1.96 * sqrt((fit.mean * (1 - fit.mean)) / number.seq)
number.ll999 <- fit.mean - 3.29 * sqrt((fit.mean * (1 - fit.mean)) / number.seq)
number.ul999 <- fit.mean + 3.29 * sqrt((fit.mean * (1 - fit.mean)) / number.seq)

dfCI <- data.frame(
  number.seq, number.ll95, number.ul95,
  number.ll999, number.ul999, fit.mean
)





p <- ggplot(df, aes(x = Positive, y = rate)) +
  geom_point(aes(label = `Sub-district`),
             alpha = 0.4,
             size = 0.9) +
  geom_line(data = dfCI,
            aes(x = number.seq, y = number.ll95),
            linewidth = 0.4,
            colour = "grey40",
            linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(data = dfCI,
            aes(x = number.seq, y = number.ul95),
            linewidth = 0.4,
            colour = "grey40",
            linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(data = dfCI,
            aes(x = number.seq, y = number.ll999),
            linewidth = 0.4,
            colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(data = dfCI,
            aes(x = number.seq, y = number.ul999),
            linewidth = 0.4,
            colour = "grey40") +
  geom_hline(data = dfCI,
             aes(yintercept = fit.mean),
             linewidth = 0.4,
             colour = "grey40") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 0.05)) +
  annotate("text", x = 1, y = -0.13, label = "95%", size = 3, colour = "grey40") +
  annotate("text", x = 4.5, y = -0.18, label = "99%", size = 3, colour = "grey40") +
  ggtitle("Cumulative Fatality Rate by Cumulative Number of COVID-19 Cases") +
  xlab("Cumulative Number of COVID-19 Cases") +
  ylab("Cumulative Fatality Rate") +
  theme_light() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 12),
        legend.position = c(0.91, 0.85),
        legend.title = element_text(size = 7),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 7),
        legend.background = element_rect(colour = "white"),
        legend.key = element_blank())

p












ggplotly(p, tooltip = c("label", "x", "y"))

ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = ENGLISH,

  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(name = "English grades",

ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = ENGLISH,
           y = CLASS,
           fill = stat(x))) +
  geom_density_ridges_gradient(
    scale = 3,
    rel_min_height = 0.01) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Temp. [F]",
                       option = "C") +
  scale_x_continuous(name = "English grades",
                     expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_y_discrete(name = NULL,
                   expand = expansion(add = c(0.2, 2.6))) +
  theme_ridges()










9.3.3 Mapping Probabilities onto Colour using stat_density_ridges()

ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = ENGLISH,

  stat_density_ridges(geom = "density_ridges_gradient",

  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Tail probability",
                       direction = -1) +
  theme_ridges()

    calc_ecdf = TRUE,
    quantiles = 4,

        ymax = mean + 1.96 * se),
    width = 0.2,
    colour = "black",
    alpha = 0.9,
    linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(aes(x = RACE,
                 y = mean),
             stat = "identity",
             color = "red",
             size = 1.5,
             alpha = 1) +
  labs(x = "Maths score",
       title = "95% confidence interval of mean maths score by race")










11.3.4 Interactive Error Bars

shared_df <- SharedData$new(my_sum)

bscols(
  widths = c(4, 8),
  ggplotly(
    ggplot(shared_df) +
      geom_errorbar(
        aes(x = reorder(RACE, -mean),
            ymin = mean - 2.58 * se,
            ymax = mean + 2.58 * se),
        width = 0.2,
        colour = "black",
        alpha = 0.9,
        size = 0.5) +
      geom_point(
        aes(x = RACE,
            y = mean,
            text = paste("Race:", RACE,
                         "<br>N:", n,
                         "<br>Avg. Scores:", round(mean, digits = 2),
                         "<br>99% CI:[",
                         round(mean - 2.58 * se, digits = 2), ",",
                         round(mean + 2.58 * se, digits = 2), "]")),
        stat = "identity",
        color = "red",
        size = 1.5,
        alpha = 1) +
      xlab("Race") +
      ylab("Average Scores") +
      theme_minimal() +
      theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45,
                                       vjust = 0.5,
                                       hjust = 1)) +
      ggtitle("99% Confidence interval of average maths scores by race"),
    tooltip = "text"
  ),
  DT::datatable(shared_df,
                rownames = FALSE,
                class = "compact",
                width = "100%",
                options = list(pageLength = 10,
                               scrollX = TRUE),
                colnames = c("No. of pupils",
                             "Avg Scores",
                             "Std Dev",
                             "Std Error")) %>%
    formatRound(columns = c("mean", "sd", "se"),
                digits = 2)
)

title: Hands-on Exercise 2: Beyond ggplot2 Fundamentals

2.3 Beyond ggplot2 Annotation: ggrepel

2.3.1 Problem - overlapping labels with geom_label

ggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x = MATHS,
           y = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = lm,
              linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_label(aes(label = ID),
             hjust = .5,
             vjust = -.5) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 100),
                  ylim = c(0, 100)) +
  ggtitle("English scores versus Maths scores for Primary 3")

ggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x = MATHS,
           y = ENGLISH)) +

  geom_smooth(method = lm,
              linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_label_repel(aes(label = ID),

  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 100),
                  ylim = c(0, 100)) +
  ggtitle("English scores versus Maths scores for Primary 3")

title: Hands-on Exercise 2: Beyond ggplot2 Fundamentals
text:
2.5 Beyond Single Graph: patchwork

2.5.1 Create individual plots

p1 <- ggplot(data = exam_data,
             aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20,
                 boundary = 100,
                 color = "grey25",
                 fill = "grey90") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 100)) +
  ggtitle("Distribution of Maths scores")

p2 <- ggplot(data = exam_data,
             aes(x = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20,
                 boundary = 100,
                 color = "grey25",
                 fill = "grey90") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 100)) +
  ggtitle("Distribution of English scores")

p3 <- ggplot(data = exam_data,
             aes(x = MATHS,
                 y = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = lm,
              linewidth = 0.5) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 100),
                  ylim = c(0, 100)) +
  ggtitle("English vs Maths scores")



2.5.2 Combining two plots side by side

p1 + p2










2.5.3 Combining three plots

(p1 / p2) | p3










2.5.4 Creating composite figure with tag

((p1 / p2) | p3) +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = "I")










2.5.5 Creating figure with inset

p3 + inset_element(p2,
                   left = 0.02,
                   bottom = 0.7,
                   right = 0.5,
                   top = 1)










2.5.6 Composite figure with patchwork and ggtheme

patchwork <- (p1 / p2) | p3
patchwork & theme_economist()

title: ISSS608-VAA
text: Welcome to ISSS608 Visual Analytics and Applications. In this website you will find coursework prepared for this course.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
Study Goal

Identify which factors weaken portfolio profitability.
Identify which factors increase portfolio volatility.
Translate the findings into underwriting and pricing actions.


This study uses a real motor insurance portfolio from Spain covering 2022 to 2024. The analysis focuses on profitability through loss ratio and on volatility through claim frequency and claim severity. The goal is not just to describe the portfolio, but to pinpoint the most actionable risk segments for an insurer.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
Contents

Data and preparation
Portfolio structure
Profitability findings
Volatility findings
Recommendations


The deck moves from context to action. I first summarise the data and the derived analytical measures, then show how the portfolio is structured, followed by the key profitability and volatility patterns. I close with recommendations that an underwriting or portfolio management team could use immediately.

The dataset contains 354,140 rows and almost 186,000 unique insured IDs. I derived the main insurance performance metrics directly from premium, incurred loss and exposure fields. Because a small number of rows had zero premium and zero exposure, I kept them in the base dataset but excluded them from ratio calculations to avoid invalid values.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
Portfolio Structure


The structure of the portfolio matters because the dominant products have the greatest influence on overall results. Most exposure sits in CC and COMP_E. That means any profitability problem within comprehensive or broad third-party products can materially affect total portfolio performance.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
Profitability Distribution


Median loss ratio is zero because many policies have no claims.
Exposure-weighted loss ratio is about 70%.
The tail remains important for volatility management.


The distribution is strongly right-skewed. Many policies have no claims in the observed period, which drives the median to zero. However, the right tail is operationally important because a relatively small share of claim-heavy policies drives volatility and can erode profitability quickly.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
Policy Type Drives Profitability


Policy type is the clearest performance separator. COMP_N has the highest loss ratio and the highest claim frequency, followed by COMP_E. TP performs best. This indicates that coverage breadth and pricing structure are critical drivers of portfolio profitability and should be a first management priority.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
2024 Deterioration


The 2024 results are worse across most product lines, not just one isolated segment. The most serious issue is COMP_N, which crosses the breakeven threshold. This suggests that management should treat the deterioration as a current pricing or claims-cost problem, rather than a purely historical issue.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
Underwriting Signals Matter


Two operational signals stand out. First, favourable bonus scores are associated with lower claim frequency, which makes them a strong underwriting input. Second, annual billing performs better than semiannual and quarterly billing. Instalment plans may be acting as a proxy for higher-risk behaviour or weaker policyholder quality.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
section: Volatility is Highest in Comprehensive Covers
text:
Volatility is Highest in Comprehensive Covers


Volatility is not only a frequency story. The claim severity distributions show that comprehensive products also carry wider and heavier severity tails. That means these segments contribute more uncertainty to earnings, even when average loss ratios alone do not fully capture the problem.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
Recommendations

Reprice or redesign COMP_N and COMP_E.
Tighten renewal controls for portfolio business.
Encourage annual billing and review instalment surcharges.
Use bonus score and vehicle value more aggressively in segmentation.
Investigate the 2024 deterioration immediately.


The recommendations follow directly from the visual evidence. Product redesign and pricing review should start with comprehensive lines. Existing portfolio business needs closer monitoring than new business. Billing structure can be used as a practical management lever, and the 2024 deterioration deserves urgent diagnosis to separate pricing inadequacy from inflation or claim mix changes.
